series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 1/1] mm, swap: only prefer nonfull clusters on synchronous devices
series_items.patch_summary: This patch partially reverts a previous change that preferred non-full clusters over free ones for swap allocation, except on synchronous devices like zram where contiguity doesn't matter. It introduces a new helper function to determine whether to prefer free clusters based on the device's flags.

review_comments.author: Nhat Pham
review_comments.summary: LGTM for the most part, with a suggestion to also prefer non-full clusters for zswap and a best-effort check of the folio's cgroup's zswappability.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Thu, Nov 5, 2026 at 8:51 AM Alexandre Ghiti <alex@ghiti.fr> wrote:
>
> Commit 9a42aed48421 ("mm, swap: prefer nonfull over free clusters") made
> allocations fill the nonfull clusters of their order before taking a
> free one, on every device without discard. Since commit 3cedb745d354
> ("mm: clarify the folio_free_swap() for do_swap_page()"), an exclusive
> write fault frees the swap slot, so a workload that rewrites swapped out
> memory leaves holes in full clusters, which then go back on the nonfull
> list. Reclaim allocates slots one folio at a time, so a batch of folios
> gets scattered over those holes, its writes can't be merged and it is
> written with many small requests.
>
> So partially revert commit 9a42aed48421 ("mm, swap: prefer nonfull over
> free clusters") and prefer free clusters again, except on synchronous
> devices like zram: they don't merge I/O, so the contiguity of the slots
> doesn't matter to them, and filling the holes first keeps the free
> clusters for large folios.
>
> Fixes: 9a42aed48421 ("mm, swap: prefer nonfull over free clusters")
> Suggested-by: Kairui Song <kasong@tencent.com>
> Signed-off-by: Alexandre Ghiti <alex@ghiti.fr>

LGTM for the most part:

Reviewed-by: Nhat Pham <nphamcs@gmail.com>

Quick comment below:

> ---
>  mm/swapfile.c | 19 +++++++++++++------
>  1 file changed, 13 insertions(+), 6 deletions(-)
>
> diff --git a/mm/swapfile.c b/mm/swapfile.c
> index 189f04d8838f..1c1b5d0b724a 100644
> --- a/mm/swapfile.c
> +++ b/mm/swapfile.c
> @@ -973,6 +973,17 @@ static bool __swap_cluster_alloc_entries(struct swap_info_struct *si,
>         return true;
>  }
>
> +/*
> + * Prefer a new cluster over a nonfull one if the device needs discard, to
> + * spread out the writes, or if it is not synchronous, to keep the slots
> + * of a swapout batch contiguous so that its writes can be merged.
> + */
> +static bool swap_prefer_free_cluster(struct swap_info_struct *si)
> +{
> +       return (si->flags & SWP_PAGE_DISCARD) ||
> +              !(si->flags & SWP_SYNCHRONOUS_IO);
> +}

Side note - I wonder if it's worth it to also prefer non-full clusters
for zswap as well?

It's a bit tricky, but I suppose you can do a best-effort check of the
folio's cgroup's zswappability?

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch addresses a performance regression in the Linux kernel, specifically related to swap I/O operations on synchronous devices like NVMe partitions. The issue arises from two commits: one that prefers non-full clusters over free ones and another that frees swap slots on exclusive write faults. This leads to scattered writes and increased read requests, resulting in decreased throughput. The patch proposes a solution by only preferring non-full clusters on synchronous devices, which improves performance metrics such as device read and write requests per transaction and throughput.

Reviewer Nhat Pham suggested considering also preferring non-full clusters for zswap devices, noting it would require a best-effort check of the folio's cgroup's zswappability.

patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH] mm/memory: refuse to map page cache folios that are not uptodate

version_history.subject: [PATCH] mm/memory: refuse to map page cache folios that are not uptodate

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch prevents the Linux kernel from mapping page cache folios that are not uptodate, which can leak stale memory to userspace. The patch adds a function `file_folio_not_uptodate` to check if a folio is uptodate and refuses the mapping if it's not. This change affects the `finish_fault` and `do_set_pmd` functions in the kernel's memory management code. The goal of this patch is to prevent silent leaks of stale memory, which can occur when userspace maps page cache folios that have not been properly read in or cleared.

patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH] crash: keep crashkernel CMA pages reserved if activation fails

version_history.subject: [PATCH] crash: keep crashkernel CMA pages reserved if activation fails

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch modifies the crashkernel memory reservation mechanism to keep CMA pages reserved even if their activation fails. This ensures that kernel data written to these pages is not overwritten by the crash kernel and remains available in the dump. The change adds a new function call, cma_reserve_pages_on_error(), which marks the areas as reserved when activation fails.

review_comments.author: Bradley Morgan
review_comments.summary: The reviewer noted that the patch's behavior of marking crashkernel CMA areas as reserved on activation error would also occur under every bitmap_zalloc() failure, and asked if this is accounted for.
review_comments.raw_body:
You do know that this will activate under every bitmap_zalloc() failure,
right? Is that accounted for?

review_comments.author: Usama Arif (author)
review_comments.summary: The author addressed Bradley Morgan's concern about the crashkernel CMA pages being released when activation fails, explaining that keeping them reserved ensures the first kernel doesn't overwrite or lose data from the vmcore. The author confirmed this is the intended behavior and mentioned an alternative approach in fadump.
review_comments.raw_body:
Yes, that's intended. By the time cma_activate_area() runs, the range is
already in crashk_cma_ranges[], so the crash kernel will use it no matter
why activation failed. Keeping the pages reserved is the only way to make
sure the first kernel has nothing there that gets overwritten or goes
missing from the vmcore; the area then behaves like a regular
crashkernel= reservation of the same size.

fadump made the same choice; it is what cma_reserve_pages_on_error() was
added for in commit 27d121d0ec6d ("mm/cma: provide option to opt out
from exposing pages on activation failure").

The bitmap is one bit per page (32 KiB per GiB with 4K pages) and is
allocated at core_initcall, so a failure there is very unlikely.

The alternative is to give the memory back and to drop the
range from crashk_cma_ranges[] when activation fails, leaving the crash
kernel with less memory than requested. I do think that is acceptable as
well. But we do need either whats done in this patch or give the memory
back. Happy to send the alternative as v2 is everyone thinks that the
better way forward.

review_comments.author: Mikhail Zaslonko
review_comments.summary: The reviewer noted that the patch's fix for crashkernel CMA areas crossing the 2G boundary on s390 is insufficient, as it only addresses the issue when movablecore= is set, and instead suggested keeping the original version of the patch which marks the areas with cma_reserve_pages_on_error() to reserve the pages even if activation fails. Additionally, they mentioned a second problem in the same loop where all areas are named 'crashkernel', breaking CMA sysfs and debugfs entries when there are multiple areas.
review_comments.raw_body:
s390 hits this without movablecore= (adding the s390 maintainers and
linux-s390) since ZONE_DMA ends at 2G here.
CMA tries to reserve areas above 4G first, but falls back to lower
memory when it doesn't fit, so a cma area can end up across the 2G boundary.
I ran into this while adding crashkernel=,cma support for s390, which I
will post soon, and came up with the same fix.

About dropping the range instead, as you offered for v2: I'd keep this
version. With the range dropped, the kdump kernel gets less memory than
configured, and that only shows at crash time. With this patch, the
the first kernel 'loses' the memory as with a regular crashkernel= reservation
of the same size.

There is a second problem in the same loop: all areas are named
"crashkernel", which breaks the CMA sysfs and debugfs entries when
there are several. I've sent a separate fix for that:

https://lore.kernel.org/r/20261106104309.3669583-1-zaslonko@linux.ibm.com

Reviewed-by: Mikhail Zaslonko <zaslonko@linux.ibm.com>
Tested-by: Mikhail Zaslonko <zaslonko@linux.ibm.com>

review_comments.author: Usama Arif (author)
review_comments.summary:
Author agreed that losing memory in the first kernel is preferable, as it forces a fix before a crash occurs.

Author acknowledged Mikhail's feedback that the patch does not handle the case where crashkernel CMA areas are reserved but activation fails, agreed to add a check in v2.
review_comments.raw_body:
Yes, I do agree with this. Losing memory in first kernel is preferrable
and it will then force someone to fix whatever is broken rather than
finding out when their kernel crashes.

---

Thanks for testing and reviewing!

Usama
